title: Is Outbreak & Biohazard Office Decontamination Included in Standard Cleaning or Billed Extra?
seoTitle: Extra Charge for COVID & Norovirus Outbreak Decontamination vs Base
metaDescription: Find out when COVID and norovirus outbreak decontamination is an extra charge ($0.20-$0.85/sq ft) vs included in base janitorial retainers. Compare quotes now.
excerpt: Most commercial janitorial contracts include routine high-touch surface wiping in the monthly retainer but strictly exclude confirmed outbreak and biohazard decontamination. Learn how to audit your scope of work to prevent surprise emergency work-order markups.
quickAnswer: In 95% of standard US commercial janitorial agreements, confirmed COVID-19, norovirus, or biohazard outbreak decontamination is billed as an extra add-on project charge ($0.20 to $0.85 per sq ft, or $55 to $95 per specialty labor hour with a $250 to $450 minimum dispatch fee). Base monthly cleaning retainers ($0.07 to $0.15 per sq ft for mid-size offices) only cover routine nightly touchpoint wiping with general-purpose disinfectants, excluding OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen PPE, EPA List G virucidal dwell protocols, electrostatic fogging, and regulated bio-waste disposal.

blocks.text: The Contract Boundary: Routine Touchpoint Wiping vs. Outbreak Decontamination

The most common billing dispute during a workplace illness cluster stems from ambiguous terminology in the janitorial Scope of Work (SOW). Facility managers frequently see 'nightly disinfection of restroom fixtures, breakroom counters, and entry door hardware' listed in their base monthly contract and assume the vendor is obligated to perform deep decontamination at no extra charge when three employees test positive for COVID-19 or an acute norovirus incident occurs in a restroom corridor.

In commercial janitorial underwriting, routine nightly cleaning is priced around high-speed production benchmarks—typically 3,500 square feet per labor hour under ISSA time standards, billed at standard janitor wages ($35 to $65 per billable hour). At that pace, a cleaner spends 15 to 30 seconds wiping a conference table or door push-plate with a quaternary ammonium spray. True outbreak and biohazard decontamination requires slowing production down to 800 to 1,500 square feet per hour, suiting technicians in Tyvek coveralls and N95/half-face respirators, observing strict 3-to-10-minute wet chemical dwell times, and running electrostatic sprayers or ULV foggers. Because the labor intensity and chemical liability triple, contractors classify outbreak remediation as an out-of-scope specialty add-on.

blocks.text: Why Vendors Exclude Norovirus and Biohazard Events From Fixed Monthly Retainers

A standard 10,000-square-foot office cleaned 3 times per week (13.0 visits per month at the 4.333 weeks/month commercial standard) typically carries a base monthly retainer between $1,400 and $2,200 ($0.14 to $0.22 per square foot per month, or roughly $0.07 to $0.12 per square foot per visit with a 0.95 frequency multiplier). That monthly fee leaves the janitorial contractor with a net operating margin of 8% to 14%.

If a norovirus outbreak hits that same 10,000-square-foot suite, a single terminal decontamination deployment requires 12 to 18 man-hours of specialty certified labor ($55 to $95/hour), $180 to $320 in ready-to-use EPA List G sporicidal chemistry and disposable PPE suits, plus a supervisor sign-off. A single unbilled outbreak event costing $1,200 to $2,100 would wipe out the contractor's entire profit margin on that building for 6 to 9 months. Consequently, legal boilerplate in almost every national and regional janitorial agreement explicitly excludes 'pandemic response, communicable disease remediation, and regulated biological spills' from the base monthly fee.

blocks.title: Watch Out for 'Emergency Mobilization' Price Gouging
blocks.text: If your contract lacks a pre-negotiated Outbreak Rate Card schedule, vendors responding to a sudden exposure notice can legally bill ad-hoc emergency rates of $0.55 to $0.95 per square foot plus a $350 to $500 same-day dispatch fee. Always attach a fixed Unit Price Schedule to your master services agreement before signing.
Hidden Consumable and Waste-Handling Charges During an Outbreak

When auditing outbreak decontamination invoices, property managers are often surprised by secondary charges for paper goods, trash liners, and dispenser purging. During a confirmed norovirus or severe gastrointestinal cluster, open uncovered toilet tissue rolls and contaminated deskside wastebaskets inside the isolation zone must be stripped, double-bagged, and replaced to prevent cross-contamination.

items: Enclosed Roll Towel Systems: Touchless enclosed systems loaded with Scott Pro Hard Roll Paper Towels 1.75-Inch Core (6-Case) shield the internal 1,150-foot paper supply from airborne aerosol droplets and electrostatic misting, preventing the vendor from condemning and billing for replacement paper stock after fogging.

High-Capacity Restroom Tissue: Keeping high-traffic stalls stocked with Scott Essential Jumbo Roll Toilet Paper 2-Ply (12-Case) inside covered ABS dispensers reduces how frequently daytime porters must open and handle exposed rolls during peak flu and norovirus months.

Rapid Double-Lining of Workstation Waste: Outbreak protocols require pulling and tying off every deskside receptacle in the affected department regardless of fill level. Supplying crews with Boardwalk 24x33 Low-Cost Office Deskside Trash Can Liners (1000-Case) provides 8-micron high-density coreless rolls that allow rapid double-bagging of tissues and PPE wipes without paying a 40% contractor consumable markup.

blocks.text: When Does It Make Sense to Bundle Decontamination Into Your Base Retainer?

While 5x-weekly general corporate offices should keep outbreak decontamination as a pre-priced per-event add-on, three specific facility profiles achieve lower total annual cost by folding periodic electrostatic or high-level virucidal sanitation directly into their monthly retainer:

items.name: 1. High-Density Call Centers and 24/7 Operations Floors
items.text: Where 100+ employees share headsets, chairs, and dual-monitor bays across rotating shifts, folding a weekly or biweekly electrostatic misting pass into the base contract adds just $0.03 to $0.05 per square foot per month—roughly 50% cheaper than ordering individual project work orders.

items.name: 2. Medical-Adjacent Administrative Suites and Billing Offices
items.text: Administrative wings connected to outpatient clinics or urgent care centers experience elevated foot traffic from symptomatic visitors. Include daily EPA List G restroom and lobby disinfection directly in the base SOW rather than paying per-incident upgrades.

items.name: 3. Multi-Tenant Class A Lobby and Amenity Floors
items.text: Property managers overseeing shared fitness centers, conference centers, and ground-floor security turnstiles often amortize quarterly deep floor care and quarterly outbreak misting together into the CAM (Common Area Maintenance) base budget at $0.03 to $0.06 per square foot per month.

blocks.text: How to Write an 'Outbreak Rate Card Rider' Into Your Janitorial RFP

Before awarding a commercial cleaning contract, require every finalist to populate a binding Contingency Rate Card in Exhibit B of the agreement. This eliminates negotiation friction when HR reports a positive case at 4:00 PM on a Wednesday and leadership wants the floor sanitized before 7:00 AM Thursday.

faqs.q: Can my janitorial company charge extra to clean up vomit or biological spills in an office restroom?
faqs.a: Yes, in almost all standard commercial office contracts. Once a bodily fluid spill involves suspected norovirus or bloodborne pathogens under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030, standard night cleaners without bloodborne-pathogen training, proper PPE, and biohazard disposal kits are instructed not to touch it. Contractors typically bill $250 to $450 as an emergency biohazard callout unless your contract specifically includes minor biological spill response in the daytime porter or nightly scope.

faqs.q: How much should an electrostatic spraying add-on cost if my regular crew performs it during their scheduled shift?
faqs.a: When your incumbent janitorial crew performs electrostatic disinfection at the end of their regular nightly shift—eliminating separate travel time and emergency dispatch mobilization—the add-on cost should drop to $0.10 to $0.18 per square foot (or $150 to $250 for a 1,500-to-2,500 sq ft zone), covering the specialty chemical cost and 1.5 to 3 additional man-hours.

faqs.q: What documentation should I require before paying an extra outbreak decontamination invoice?
faqs.a: Require four verification items attached to the work-order invoice: (1) the EPA Registration Number and Safety Data Sheet (SDS) confirming List N or List G efficacy, (2) time-stamped check-in/check-out logs showing sufficient labor hours to meet label contact dwell times, (3) a floor plan map marking the exact square footage treated, and (4) confirmation that glass and polished metal hardware were wiped clear of corrosive chemical residue.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to buy our own electrostatic sprayer or pay contractor add-on fees?
faqs.a: Buying a commercial handheld electrostatic sprayer costs $600 to $1,400, which helps if you employ in-house facility maintenance staff trained in respirator safety and chemical dilution. However, for leased offices relying on outsourced janitorial vendors, liability insurance (COI pollution and chemical damage exclusions) usually prohibits contracted cleaners from operating client-owned chemical dispersal hardware.
